generatedProse.concept-context: In your subject, a strong prompt still rests on three parts. You give the tool a role to play, a clear function to carry out, and the context you bring: your level, your module, and the terms you keep mixing up. The more precise those three parts, the less generic the answer. A vague request earns a vague reply; a specific one makes the tool work on your actual problem.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who want help revising research methods, each writing one prompt for the same AI tool.

{{learner-a}} types a single line: explain research methods. The answer is long, generic, and pitched at no particular level. It never mentions {{learner-a}}'s module, it muddles the very terms {{learner-a}} finds hard, and it offers nothing to practise. {{learner-a}} reads it, feels no clearer, and has done no real thinking.

{{learner-b}} builds the prompt in three parts. The role is a supportive tutor for a first-year. The function is to explain the difference between qualitative and quantitative methods, then set five short questions and hide the answers. The context is a social sciences student who keeps confusing methods with methodology. The reply is pitched right, names the trap, and gives {{learner-b}} something to attempt.

Both asked about the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} gave the tool a role, a function and a context, and so got an answer that made them think.
generatedProse.summary: A strong prompt is built, not blurted. You set a role, a clear function and the context you bring, and you ask for the method rather than the finished answer. You can now construct a prompt from those three parts, combine the habits that make a tool think with you, and build a prompt for your own work that you can justify. Next, you will learn the moves that turn one prompt into a productive dialogue.

check.body: In the worked example, why did the second prompt produce a more useful answer than the first?

items.text: It gave the tool a role, a specific function and the student's own context.
It was written in more formal and confident language.
It asked the tool for a longer answer.
It used the exact wording from the module handbook.

feedback.correct: That's right. A role, a clear function and real context make the answer specific and push you to think.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second prompt added that the first one left out.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The second prompt supplied a role, a function and the student's context. Length, tone and borrowed wording were not what made the difference.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
